    #20280. What it will take for CMOs to reach the next frontier of AI-driven growth

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1081 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    What it will take for CMOs to reach the next frontier of AI-driven growth

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • In a recent development, CMOs at the largest enterprise brands across consumer goods, financial services, B2B and more are all struggling with the same thing: more AI technology has not translated into more business growth.
    • In a recent development, but a few CMOs are doing it differently.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    In a recent development, CMOs at the largest enterprise brands across consumer goods, financial services, B2B and more are all struggling with the same thing: more AI technology has not translated into more business growth. They’re stuck chasing efficiency gains, funding tools that optimize tasks inside functional silos, running pilots that go nowhere and delegating AI decisions to IT teams.

    In a recent development, but a few CMOs are doing it differently. Eric Schwartz, CMO of The Clorox Tech giant, told me his marketers are building AI systems that produce highly optimized product content. They’re encoding brand voice, compliance guardrails and seasonal context into agents that work across every brand in their portfolio. Their goal isn’t to save time on doing what human writers can already do. Instead, they want to codify, scale and orchestrate the expertise that increases relevance, engagement and conversion with consumers. That’s a growth play.

    This is an operating-model decision that the CMO has to own: give marketers the strategic, system-building work and shift execution to AI agents. That takes much more than a chatbot built for a solo work experience.

    “I tell everyone that tries to pitch me about AI capabilities that the last thing I need is a 14th chatbot to save our marketers time,” Schwartz stated. “What I need is interoperable functionality.”.

    Industry observers note that schwartz isn’t alone. A vanguard of marketers are charting the frontier of AI-native marketing. To do this requires three fundamental shifts.

    In a recent development, employees are becoming more efficient with AI, but report that leaders aren’t asking them to reinvest the productivity gains into strategic work; they’re just expected to produce more output. Boston Consulting Group found that 66% of frontline employees receive limited or no guidance on using saved time, and more than half don’t reinvest it into strategic work.

    Measuring AI success solely on efficiency invites efficiency’s reward: a smaller budget.

    For example, one CMO’s AI-powered content system is saving the tech giant 500 hours a month. But the company’s CFO saw the dashboard and asked: “If marketing can do this with 500 fewer hours, why does the budget stay the same?” The dashboard was supposed to prove value. Instead, it made the case for a cut.

    Sources indicate that A marketing team at a regulated financial services tech giant chose a different approach. The team was losing 360 hours a week to legal review bottlenecks, manual multi-channel content creation and constant product updates across 800-plus references. The team built a system with compliance encoded into the workflow and distribution automated across 25 channels. The result: 360 hours freed up weekly, 90% less editing time and zero agency spend.

    The marketing team reinvested those hours into producing an award-winning ad campaign, not producing more of the same content. In a category where most consumers can’t name three financial lenders, breaking through the sameness drove brand recall, pipeline and market share. The system handled the production, but the humans did the work that won.

    The AI opportunity isn’t time saved. Frontier CMOs reinvest that time in architecture, curation and orchestration: designing agentic workflows, encoding brand voice and steering the system to drive growth. The humans who know best what makes their brand different turn saved time into a real advantage.

    It has been revealed that historically, marketing and revenue have operated on separate tracks. In B2B, marketing fills the top of the funnel and hands off to sales. In consumer brands, marketing creates content while commerce manages the shelf. In financial services, brand marketing and the advisors who own the relationship rarely connect. In most organizations, no single team owns the moments that decide the sale.

    Sixty-seven percent of B2B buyers now prefer a rep-free experience, according to data from Gartner. Consumers and bank customers are doing their own research too. In financial services, buyers are asking AI tools for recommendations before they ever talk to an advisor. These buyers aren’t waiting for a handoff.At the frontier, there are no handoffs. AI agents carry customer data, market signals and brand and compliance context between marketing and revenue teams in real time. Context doesn’t die at a cross-functional boundary. It compounds.

    Schwartz described what this looks like at Clorox. The manufacturer’s media ecosystem spans retail media, e-commerce and traditional retail, and the goal is to connect performance back to sales — or to the signals that point to sales. Most marketing organizations stop at creating and deploying campaigns. Schwartz wants that signal flowing back to show where to lean in and scale and to shape what gets created next. By closing that loop, a media budget compounds into growth instead of disappearing.

    According to recent reports, A CMO recently told me his organization has 40 active pilots, all marked green. Everything worked in the lab, but nothing survived contact with the organization. IT loved the tools, but marketing couldn’t use them.

    Recent findings suggest that this happens when AI adoption is delegated to IT. The CMO sponsors the budget but doesn’t own the transformation. In Writer’s 2026 survey, more than half of CMOs (52.3%) reported “significant knowledge gaps” about AI. Gartner predicts that by 2027, lack of AI literacy will rank among the top three reasons CMOs are replaced.

    It has been revealed that at the frontier, the CMO owns the entire marketing AI agenda: selecting tools, redesigning workflows and deciding what should remain human-led. That means making AI adoption a cultural shift, not a software rollout. And that can’t be delegated.

    Schwartz is an example of what this looks like in practice. He made AI adoption his own rather than delegating it to an innovation team or task force.

    It has been revealed that the CMOs making progress are changing how the work gets done, moving from traditional marketing operations toward a new model of driving growth with AI. They aren’t simply doing the same work with AI layered on top, but reimagining foundational structures, systems and strategies for a new era of marketing. The frontier isn’t a place a CMO arrives at. It’s the way a CMO operates.Partner insights from Writer.

    Marketers use creator, influencer and tastemaker interchangeably, but the industry still hasn’t settled on what the labels mean.

    In Q3 earnings, The Trade Desk’s leadership reveals it is searching for answers.

    Japanese holdco appointed Mike Nakamura as entertainment and sport chief, as media revenues slip in most markets.

    Tech Report: Anatomy of an influencer marketing deal

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Ever wonder how an influencer marketing deal gets negotiated?
    • In a live Digiday Podcast recording during the recent Creator Strategies virtual event, YSL Beauty’s Hadley Musinsky and Night’s Sophie Bressler broke down how deals between brands and influencers come together.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Ever wonder how an influencer marketing deal gets negotiated? Well, you’re in luck.

    In a live Digiday Podcast recording during the recent Creator Strategies virtual event, YSL Beauty’s Hadley Musinsky and Night’s Sophie Bressler broke down how deals between brands and influencers come together. Step one usually starts with the brand.

    “Whenever we have a launch or a business priority, we’ll talk through where do we need support, who do we want support from and what does that really look like. Then, as the influencer lead, we’ll talk through or present ideas, concepts, creator names that I think would be such a perfect fit for the product. And I will then reach out to someone like Sophie, who I’ve had a great relationship with for over 10 years now,” said Musinsky, director of influence and advocacy at YSL Beauty.

    Recent findings suggest that then the ball is in the creator’s court, or at least the creator’s talent manager, such as Bressler. Brief in hand, she looks for the brand’s objective to identify the creators best suited to the campaign.

    “If Hadley states to me, ‘We’re really looking to drive sales’, I don’t want to put forward a client who doesn’t have a history of strong link clicks on Instagram Stories,” Bressler mentioned.

    From there, the two sides go back and forth to hash out details, including exclusivity, usage rights and eventually payment terms.

    “The payment terms don’t get ironed out until we get to the contracting stage,” noted Bressler, who delved into details of those discussions in the episode, along with Musinsky who shared YSL Beauty and parent firm’s L’Oréal’s payment terms.

    Here are a few highlights from the conversation, which have been edited for length and clarity.

    It has been revealed that musinsky: “We usually don’t include links, so we’re not tracking to that extent. Of course, we want to see a spike in sales. But there’s never this goal [of an] exact percentage-increase number. For us, it’s usually more of an awareness play, or as we call it, a virality moment of starting a conversation, having that video or multiple videos perform really well and then seeing other creators feed off of it. Usually that’s our goal.”.

    According to recent reports, bressler: “I may come to the table and say, ‘I’ve reviewed the scope of work and the creative. Based on that, this is the general starting rate for the [creator] that you’re interested in’. From there it becomes more of a conversation and a friendly negotiation. If what I’ve presented to Hadley is too high for this specific campaign, we would then work backwards to maybe scale back the scope of work, pare back the usage, remove the exclusivity, tweak the deliverables.”.

    Syndication and usage rights from the brand side.

    Industry observers note that musinsky: “For the most part, we go in with the offer asking for everything because we know we can start scaling back. If we’re looking for an Instagram post or TikTok, we’ll ask for syndication so that it’s posted across both platforms or even three platforms that will include YouTube Shorts. And then in terms of usage, we’ll usually ask for two weeks paid upfront. We do love to boost content. I think it’s also beneficial for the creator. That’s us putting spend behind it and it running through their account as an ad.”.

    Exclusivity and usage rights from the creator side.

    Industry observers note that bressler: “When it comes to paid usage, what is the perceived exclusivity there? Even if there is not technical exclusivity and my client could work with [a separate] luxe beauty brand the next day, if YSL Beauty is running paid ads with my client in it, another luxe beauty brand may not want to collaborate with [the creator] because they think they must be off the table because they’re working with YSL Beauty. We as reps need to understand what other opportunities are on the table at that specific time and weigh the opportunity cost against the desired scope of work in full.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    What if your brand’s biggest opportunity was completely hidden within your existing assets?

    In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, Jenny Rooney sits down with AARP CMO Anna Banks to unpack the challenge of repositioning a brand with more than 125 million Americans aged 50 and over in its sights.

    Anna gets into why the second half of life deserves a different story, why celebrity partnerships need to lead somewhere meaningful, and why AARP’s next chapter depends on connecting the many touchpoints it already owns.

    Anna also shares how performance marketing translates into a mission-driven organization, what makes a partnership genuinely valuable, and why good leadership starts with listening.

    Anna Banks is the Chief Marketing Officer at AARP with over 30 years of marketing experience across brand strategy, digital, ecommerce, and performance marketing under her belt.

    Her career has taken her from Lotus Development Corporation and 15 years on the agency side to Walmart eCommerce, Fairtrade USA, and Sephora. At AARP, she’s bringing those experiences together to help reposition a legacy brand and connect more meaningfully with the 125 million Americans aged 50 and over.

    Recent findings suggest that her approach brings together consumer insight, brand engagement and performance-driven conversion. In this conversation, she shares how AARP is thinking about relevance, partnerships, technology and the opportunity to change how people think about aging.

    10:31 AARP Has a Relevance Challenge — AARP is a legacy powerhouse, but keeping membership growth in step with the changing population means making sure more people understand how relevant the organization is to their lives.

    It has been revealed that 12:28 The Second Half of Life Is the Most Creative Act — What if people stopped thinking about the second half of life as a period of decline? Anna shares how AARP wants people to see it as a chance to figure out what really matters and what drives them.

    13:49 Celebrity Gets Attention. The Challenges Keep It. — From Eva Longoria to George Clooney, celebrity partnerships help AARP catch people’s attention. But the stories around caregiving, representation and aging are what make those partnerships matter.

    15:51 Your Brand’s Assets Need to Work Together — Anna talks about the opportunity to connect AARP’s magazine, website and other channels, and why the organization needs to show up wherever people are already consuming media.

    17:11 Stop Underestimating the 50+ Audience — Think people over 50 aren’t using mobile search or smart TVs? Anna challenges those assumptions and points out that the average 50+ consumer uses seven tech devices.

    26:22 Performance Marketing Has a Place at AARP — Anna explains how her experience at Sephora translates to AARP’s membership acquisition and advertising model, and why performance marketing is just as relevant in a mission-driven organization.

    Jenny Rooney is Chief Brand and Community Officer, leading strategy for the overall ADWEEK brand as well as the ways in which we serve and support our audiences with high-value content, products, partnerships and experiences, notably through our community programs such as Marketing Vanguard.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Director of Technology Partnerships to lead the teams responsible for growing Supabase through technology integrations and our marketplace ecosystem.

    You’ll bring together two complementary motions: partnerships that embed Supabase into the products developers already use, and a marketplace that helps developers discover and connect complementary technologies to their Supabase projects. Your job is to turn both into durable sources of revenue, adoption, and customer value.

    Industry observers note that reporting to the Head of Partnerships, you’ll lead and develop the Integrations and Marketplace teams, set their commercial strategy, and work hands-on with our most important partners. A central part of the role is working closely with AI labs to build strategic relationships, develop integrations, and bring joint opportunities to market. You’ll partner closely with Product, Engineering, Sales, Marketing, and Finance to take integrations from idea to launch—and grow their impact long after launch.

    In a recent development, this role is based in the San Francisco Bay Area, where you’ll build relationships with leading AI, developer tools, and infrastructure companies. Supabase is remote-first, and you’ll work across a globally distributed team.

    Lead, coach, and develop the Integrations and Marketplace partnerships teams, including team leads and partner managers.

    Set a clear strategy for where Supabase invests across strategic technology partnerships, marketplace categories, and emerging ecosystem opportunities.

    Recent findings suggest that define team objectives, partner coverage, investment priorities, and operating cadence. Make thoughtful tradeoffs between high-touch strategic partnerships and scalable programs.

    Build a culture of ownership, commercial discipline, and strong cross-functional execution.

    Drive revenue from technology integrations through partner-driven customer acquisition, product consumption, expansion, retention, co-sell opportunities, and commercial arrangements.

    Own the commercial performance of the technology partnerships and marketplace portfolio, including forecasting and reporting on progress, risks, and return on investment.

    Build and deepen relationships with AI labs, working closely with their product, engineering, business development, and executive teams to identify and execute high-impact partnership opportunities.

    Develop executive relationships with strategic partners across developer tools, cloud, and adjacent infrastructure.

    Lead or support negotiations for complex partnerships, including integration, referral, revenue-sharing, and joint go-to-market agreements.

    Help partner managers build joint business prepares that connect partner priorities to measurable outcomes for Supabase and its customers.

    Lead and develop the Marketplace team, setting its commercial and partner strategy and holding the team accountable for outcomes.

    Guide the team in identifying the capabilities developers need, recruiting the right partners, and helping those partners launch and grow.

    Set priorities and allocate resources across strategic, high-touch partners and scalable paths for emerging and self-serve partners.

    Ensure the team works effectively with Product and Engineering on integration quality, partner onboarding, discovery, activation, and the developer experience across product surfaces.

    Enable the team to work with Marketing and Sales to launch integrations, enable teams, and drive ongoing adoption—not just announcements.

    Establish clear measures for partner-sourced and influenced pipeline, integration adoption, revenue, consumption, retention, and marketplace performance.

    Work with Finance, Data, and Partner Operations to improve attribution, reporting, forecasting, and partner revenue processes.

    Represent the voice of partners and customers in product and go-to-market planning, while aligning stakeholders around shared priorities.

    Identify risks early, remove blockers, and communicate decisions and outcomes clearly to leadership.

    Have significant experience in technology partnerships, business development, or ecosystem leadership at a developer tools, cloud, infrastructure, or SaaS tech giant.

    Have led and developed partner-facing teams, including managers or senior individual contributors, and can balance strategic direction with hands-on execution.

    Have a track record of building partnerships that produced measurable revenue, product adoption, or customer growth.

    Have negotiated complex commercial agreements and understand partnership economics, including revenue share, referrals, and consumption-based models.

    Have worked closely with Product and Engineering to ship and grow technical integrations. You can engage credibly with technical teams, including those at AI labs, even if you aren’t the person writing the code.

    Know how to build relationships with executives while earning the trust of product, engineering, and go-to-market teams.

    Use data to prioritize opportunities, assess partner performance, and make decisions when attribution is imperfect.

    Are comfortable building in an evolving environment, communicating in writing, and working asynchronously across time zones.

    Built or scaled a developer marketplace, integration ecosystem, or partner platform.

    Worked with AI LLMs, AI app builders, databases, open-source products, or developer infrastructure.

    A background in software development, with an understanding of how developers build and integrate products.

    Experience growing both a small number of strategic partnerships and a broader, scalable partner program.

    A strong network in the San Francisco Bay Area technology ecosystem.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Industry observers note that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are vital to us.

    In a recent development, once a year, the entire organization gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    According to recent reports, we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Expertise in entertainment could be the next agency C-suite superpower.
    • Nakamura’s appointment is further proof of the growing importance of entertainment expertise to major ad agencies,  as media spend concentrates around live sports and TV, film and showbiz reknit around the creator economy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Expertise in entertainment could be the next agency C-suite superpower. Takeshi Sano, the president and global CEO of Japanese agency holding manufacturer Dentsu, clearly thinks so: he’s elevated Mitsuyuki ‘Mike’ Nakamura, a former media buyer, TV producer and a 36-year Dentsu veteran, to serve as the group’s first global practice president for sports and entertainment.

    Nakamura’s appointment is further proof of the growing importance of entertainment expertise to major ad agencies,  as media spend concentrates around live sports and TV, film and showbiz reknit around the creator economy.

    “Sports and entertainment is where culture is made today, and Dentsu has a long track-record of helping brands go further than just buying space around it,” mentioned Sano in a statement.

    Nakamura has worked for Dentsu in both Thailand, as CEO of Dentsu Media, and the U.K., where he led its CX business, Dentsu X. Most recently he served as president of sports and entertainment at Dentsu Japan.

    Industry observers note that dentsu is more closely coiled with the entertainment sector than most advertising groups. It’s an investor in the upcoming Angry Birds film, which will also feature two of its clients. It has produced microdramas for P&G and recently inked a partnership with Iconic Arts to help brands create their own anime. It’s not alone in moving closer to the showbiz world, though; last week, Ogilvy launched a partnership with top talent agency CAA to use AI clones of its high profile stars in brand advertising.

    The manufacturer made the announcement the same day that it released its third-quarter earnings report. Overall organic revenue fell 3.7% and the company altered its revenue guidance for the whole of 2026 from 0.1% growth to -1%.

    In a recent development, organic growth reversed in Japan, the Americas (down 6.5%) and Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA), where income fell 7.1% due to “macro uncertainty and reduced business from major clients” hitting media revenues. Dentsu’s media revenues in the Americas have fallen 2.5% this year so far.

    Recent findings suggest that the firm’s results come amid signs of a potential slowdown in overall global advertising spending. Amazon, Google and Reddit each recorded deceleration in advertising revenues this past quarter; the former saw Amazon ad revenue growth fall from 26% in Q2, to 12% in Q3.

    But Dentsu has fared worse than its major agency group rivals. WPP’s revenue for the same period was up 0.5%, while Publicis’ rose 5%.

    And Brian Wieser, founder of Madison & Wall, suggested its revenue declines reflect its own circumstances, rather than a broader slowdown – namely the absence of Microsoft from its balance sheet. The organization lost the tech giant’s $2.67 billion global account to Publicis back in April.

    It has been revealed that “Its scale should not be underestimated,” Wieser mentioned. “It was probably by far the biggest client that Dentsu had.”.

    Spending on ad agencies is increasingly divorced from spending on advertising as a whole, Wieser added. “Marketers have been so focused on containing their non-working spending, as they characterize it, that the growth of spend on [advertising] is independent of the growth of spend on agencies,” he said.

    The bottom line is that Dentsu can’t rely on the ad spend tides to raise its boat, but must find its own way back to growth.

    In Q3 earnings, The Trade Desk’s leadership reveals it is searching for answers.

    The e-commerce giant is central for many consumer brand advertisers, but measurement changes could throw a wrench into their plans for next year.

    Sources indicate that local sports rights have gotten more complex and confusing as the regional sports network business changed. The leagues are now looking to simplify that offering.

    This Ad Tech Briefing covers the latest in ad tech and platforms for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

    Developments last week revealed that Google faces another potential antitrust setback, this time in Europe, as it prepares for the next stage of its U.S. ad tech monopoly case.

    Industry observers note that on Nov. 12, an adviser to the European Union’s highest court recommended overturning a 2024 judgment that annulled an earlier €1.49 billion ($1.7 billion) fine against Google over its AdSense for Search business.

    In a recent development, in her ⁠opinion, Advocate General Juliane Kokott argued that the EU’s General Court made legal errors when it overturned the European Commission’s original 2019 penalty. Specifically, Kokott concluded that the lower court had imposed excessive requirements on regulators when assessing whether Google’s contractual restrictions harmed competition.

    According to recent reports, the case concerns agreements Google used with publishers that displayed search advertisements through its AdSense for Search service; i.e., it involves a different business unit than the one under scrutiny in its most recent U.S. trial.

    Per the European proceedings’ plaintiffs, between 2006 and 2016, Google imposed contractual restrictions that limited those websites’ ability to display advertisements from rival search advertising providers.

    The European Commission identified three types of restrictions: exclusivity clauses preventing publishers from using competing services, placement clauses restricting where rival advertisements could appear, and provisions requiring Google’s prior approval before changes to advertising displays.

    The Commission concluded that these practices constituted a single, continuous infringement of European competition law. Google challenged the decision, and in September 2024, the General Court annulled the fine, finding that regulators had failed to examine relevant circumstances adequately, particularly the duration of Google’s contractual arrangements.

    Kokott’s opinion, published Nov. 12, argued that the General Court had placed excessive emphasis on the duration of individual agreements rather than considering their collective effect on competition.

    Sources indicate that in the accompanying press release, the court explained that regulators could assess contracts collectively to determine whether they could produce exclusionary effects. Kokott recommended setting aside the 2024 judgment and returning the case to the General Court for reconsideration.

    Importantly, the recommendation does not automatically reinstate the original fine. The opinion is nonbinding, and the Court of Justice has yet to glitch its judgment. Moreover, Kokott acknowledged that the penalty should ultimately be reduced because certain findings concerning Google’s conduct in 2016 are no longer being contested.

    Nevertheless, the opinion creates the prospect of another prolonged legal battle over Google’s advertising practices, as the development comes two months after Google avoided a forced breakup of its advertising technology business in the U.S.

    In September, federal judge Leonie Brinkema rejected the Justice Department’s proposed divestiture of Google’s AdX exchange and publisher ad server, DoubleClick for Publishers.

    Instead, the court accepted most of the government’s proposed behavioral remedies, subject to modifications. The decision shifted the focus from Google’s ownership of its advertising infrastructure to the restrictions governing how that infrastructure operates.

    Recent findings suggest that the remedies are intended to address Google’s ability to favor its own advertising products, including through changes affecting interoperability, auction transparency and access for competing ad tech companies. However, the precise obligations and their enforcement remain central questions as the parties work through the final judgment.

    Google has indicated that it intends to appeal the underlying liability decision, potentially extending the litigation beyond implementation of the behavioral remedies.

    The European and American cases concern different markets and legal questions, but both illustrate the difficulty regulators face in challenging Google’s advertising dominance.

    According to recent reports, in Europe, the courts are still examining conduct that ended a decade ago. In the U.S., the argument has moved from whether Google violated competition law to whether the remedies will materially change market behavior.

    However, even successful antitrust enforcement does not guarantee that publishers and advertisers will move their business away from Google.

    Meanwhile, last week’s proceedings demonstrated how The Trade Desk’s struggles highlight a different problem — a development that embodies the scale of the challenges independent competitors to Google, etc., face when challenging Big Tech.

    According to recent reports, on Nov. 9, The Trade Desk reported a rare quarterly revenue decline, with third-quarter sales falling approximately 0.5% to $736 million from $739 million a year earlier. While the manufacturer did beat Wall Street’s (modest) expectations, the result marked a sharp reversal for a company that had long delivered double-digit growth.

    The results underscored the difficulties facing the company during what executives have described as a transitional year. The slowdown comes amid growing competition from Amazon, shifting agency relationships and the increasing use of AI to automate media buying.

    While The Trade Desk has invested heavily in its Kokai platform and related AI capabilities, those initiatives have yet to restore its historical growth rates, with executives there also revealing how they are reconsidering how acquisitions might contribute to its next phase of growth.

    On the tech giant’s earnings call, Jeff Green, The Trade Desk, CEO, revealed leadership were taking a closer look at potential acquisitions, suggesting a more active approach to M&A than the company has historically pursued.

    For years, The Trade Desk positioned itself as an independent alternative to the advertising ecosystems operated by Google, Amazon, and other major technology companies, with this pitch a key selling point when articulating its value in the responsible use of CMOs’ media investments.

    However, its latest results demonstrate that independence alone is not enough to guarantee growth.

    It has been revealed that regulators may eventually make Google’s advertising infrastructure more accessible to competitors. But those competitors must still persuade advertisers that their platforms offer better technology, performance, and economics. The Trade Desk’s difficulties suggest that the industry’s competitive challenges extend well beyond Google’s market power.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re seeking a Technical Account Manager (TAM) to be the primary technical partner for our Team & customers after the sale, helping them adopt, operate, and get long-term value from Supabase.

    At Supabase, TAMs are the technical owners of their assigned accounts, working closely with our most valuable customers to:.

    Understand each customer’s architecture, use cases, constraints, and goals.

    Validate deployments and guide customers through onboarding and early success.

    Proactively surface risks and optimization opportunities before they become incidents.

    Coordinate internal teams on complex escalations and drive root cause analysis.

    Align Supabase capabilities with the customer’s roadmap.

    Successful TAMs are proactive, technically credible, and customer-first. TAM is a relationship, not a response channel: you’ll act as an extension of your customers’ teams and advocate on their behalf within Supabase.

    You’ll be joining our Success team, where you will be expected to lead and innovate around the following areas of responsibility:.

    Technical Ownership & Onboarding.

    Act as the technical owner for your assigned accounts, documenting environments, mapping dependencies, and tracking technical risks.

    Validate architecture and deployment aims after the sale, guide initial configuration and best practices, and make sure customers understand platform capabilities and limitations.

    Help customers reach early success milestones to shorten time to value and reduce early friction.

    Regularly review customer environments and usage patterns to identify scalability, performance, reliability, security, and compliance risks and opportunities.

    Initiative upgrades and lifecycle events, and run architecture reviews for upcoming initiatives, including capacity and growth planning, feature readiness, and early identification of technical blockers.

    Coordinate across Support and Engineering on complex or high-impact issues. TAMs are not frontline support, but provide the context, prioritization, and follow-through that drive resolution, root cause analysis, and preventative action.

    Serve as the voice of the customer to Engineering and Product, sharing specific, reproducible feedback on recurring pain points and taking part in beta and early access programs.

    Partner with Sales and Customer Success on account health and retention, with technical input on renewals, expansions, and evaluations, and early flags on risks to satisfaction.

    6+ years of relevant work experience in engineering, SRE, technical consulting, or similar, including operating production systems under real constraints.

    Strong technical depth across database internals, scalability, security posture, and infrastructure tradeoffs. You understand a customer’s architecture as well as they do, without escalating every question.

    A proactive mindset: you spot risks and optimization opportunities before the customer does, and you treat your accounts like a personal portfolio.

    Sound escalation judgment: you know when to escalate, when to resolve internally, and how to communicate clearly under pressure without creating noise.

    Sources indicate that very strong communication skills. TAMs explain complex challenges to non-technical executives and root causes to senior engineers, often in the same day.

    Awareness of how TAM performance reveals up in retention and NRR, including surfacing expansion signals and renewal risks early.

    Experience working in async or globally distributed teams.

    Industry observers note that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the firm. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    According to recent reports, supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Recent findings suggest that once a year, the entire firm gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    Sources indicate that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Sources indicate that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Recent findings suggest that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    What exactly counts as a creator? The industry still can’t agree

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, join us Dec.
    • Every brand seems to have different definitions when it comes to the creator economy.
    • It has been revealed that since the ballooning of the creator economy, marketers have been trying to standardize everything from what counts as a view, brand-creator contractual language and the framework for deal fee structures.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Every brand seems to have different definitions when it comes to the creator economy. What one brand calls a tastemaker, another labels an influencer. If marketers can’t agree on creator taxonomy, standardization — on everything from measurement to cost — may remain further away than the industry would like.

    It has been revealed that since the ballooning of the creator economy, marketers have been trying to standardize everything from what counts as a view, brand-creator contractual language and the framework for deal fee structures. According to the IAB’s latest creator economy report, at least 23% of marketers say the industry would benefit from a unified creator taxonomy.

    “That’s the blurry line. Who’s a mega influencer and who’s a celebrity? I don’t know anymore,” noted Mindy Murray, director of influencer and content at General Mills.

    Industry observers note that general Mills’ approach to creator definitions is nuanced. The highest tier is celebrity status, where partnerships often go beyond social and into product design and formula. Mega creators are positioned just below celebrity partnerships. Mid creators range from 500,000 to 1.5 million social media followers. There are super fans or brand advocates who are dedicated creators who are positing consistently on behalf of the brand. Finally, there’s friends and family, which is General Mills’ organic influencer group who also act as brand advocates.

    According to recent reports, shutterfly has a three-tier creator codification. Tastemakers are social media stars with one million or more followers. They’re handpicked for major campaigns. Content creators fall on the other end of the spectrum, having anywhere from a couple hundred to more than 2,000 social media followers. Influencers fall somewhere in between, Callie Worthington, vp of brand marketing and creative at Shutterfly, told Digiday.

    Shutterfly doesn’t have an internal pay scale that relates to its codification system. It is expected, however, that bigger creators (which could be tastemakers and influencers) command bigger budgets.

    Rothy’s shoe brand also uses the term tastemakers. However, Rothy’s creator classifications are defined less by follower count and more by their cultural relevance, said Anna Doré, vp of brand and communications at Rothy’s. A tastemaker could be a TikTok star or a Substack writer. In comparison, Rothy’s refers to affiliate creators as “the lower funnel crater and conversion types,” Doré said.

    Industry observers note that meanwhile, agencies don’t seem to go by the same guidelines. For example, VML organizes creators by their role in a campaign — salespeople, brand ambassadors, product collaborators, etc. The taxonomy isn’t as strict, Noah Eisemann, global executive director of creator and influencer at VML, told Digiday.

    “Every influencer is a creator, but not every creator is an influencer,” Eisemann mentioned.

    The creator economy has exploded to where creators aren’t just selling products on behalf of brands. They’ve been hired as actors in Super Bowl spots. They’ve been brought on as product collaborators. Some are acting as creative agencies helping brands ideate and execute creative campaigns. Kim Kardashian is as much a content creator as she is an influencer, depending on what the brand asks of her, he added.

    “The more useful standard may be a shared way of defining the role a creator is playing in a particular strategy — because that’s ultimately what should determine how we value the partnership and what success looks like,” Eisemann mentioned.

    A brand’s tiering setup influences how creators are evaluated, how their impact is measured and how they’re utilized in campaigns.

    “When expectations, budgets, and measurement rely on different assumptions, effective work can be undervalued, and investment becomes harder to justify or sustain,” mentioned Stefani Stamatiou, CEO of Americas at HYDP creator marketing agency.

    Recent findings suggest that but across the industry, there’s no conventional naming system. (Even Digiday staffers couldn’t agree on what defines a creator versus influencer.) And as more money pours into the creator economy, marketers are expecting measurement and business outcomes.

    “Greater clarity around inputs and expected outcomes would make it easier to set goals, allocate budgets, and define the role creators play within the broader advertising landscape,” Stamatiou remarked.

    A upcoming product manager role will explore ad-related monetization, suggesting the platform could make ads a bigger part of its business.

    Industry observers note that CEOs have never cared much for holdcos. Enterprise solutions, on the other hand, get a meeting.

    Marketers expect their 2026 holiday revenue to increase 1% to 31% or more in comparison to their 2025 holiday revenue.

    #20258. Industry News: Attention Is Still the Currency: Joe Marchese on Brand Building in the AI Era

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (735 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adweek ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Attention Is Still the Currency: Joe Marchese on Brand Building in the AI Era

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (735 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adweek

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, for years, marketers were told that better data would lead to better decisions.
    • Now that AI has raised the stakes again through agents that buy on the behalf of consumers, marketers may be entering a world where machines influence the buying decision before the brand ever gets a direct chance to speak.
    • This episode of The Speed of Culture podcast welcomes Joe Marchese, CEO of Human Ventures Holdings, to explore what that shift means for trust, brand, and competitive advantage.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, for years, marketers were told that better data would lead to better decisions. But Joe Marchese thinks that approach missed the more basic question: did you earn anyone’s attention in the first place?

    Now that AI has raised the stakes again through agents that buy on the behalf of consumers, marketers may be entering a world where machines influence the buying decision before the brand ever gets a direct chance to speak.

    This episode of The Speed of Culture podcast welcomes Joe Marchese, CEO of Human Ventures Holdings, to explore what that shift means for trust, brand, and competitive advantage.

    Their conversation moves from the failures of impression-driven advertising to the fiduciary problem of AI agents, why strategy becomes more valuable as optimization gets automated, and why shared cultural experiences may matter more precisely because machines cannot fully understand them.

    Joe Marchese is CEO of Human Ventures Holdings, and co-author of Human Dot AI: How the Fight for Your Attention Became the World’s Biggest Business. His career has spanned entrepreneurship, advertising technology, media and investing.

    Recent findings suggest that joe founded true[X], an advertising manufacturer built around the idea that engaged attention was more valuable than sheer impression volume, before the company was acquired by Fox. He later worked across television advertising at Fox and now invests in companies through Human Ventures, with a particular focus on how technology and AI intersect with media, culture, hospitality, and real-world human connection.

    [03:50] Data Is Useless Without Attention — Joe’s original true[X] thesis was simple: not all impressions are equal. Marketers could have enormous amounts of data about someone, but without their attention, none of it mattered. By contrast, attention alone still creates the opportunity to tell a story. His criticism of programmatic advertising is that quality attention was undervalued largely because it was harder to measure than impression volume.

    [06:42] AI Agents Need a Trust Test — Joe compares AI agents with human agents in real estate, insurance, and entertainment. If an agent is supposed to act on someone’s behalf, the user needs confidence that its incentives are aligned with theirs. The problem comes when advertising enters the equation. If an AI recommends the product that pays rather than the product that is best, the relationship starts to look less like trusted advice and more like hidden persuasion.

    In a recent development, [09:04] Invest in What Machines Can’t Understand — Joe offers CMOs a sharp filter for AI-era strategy: anything machines can understand, they will eventually optimize. That pushes competitive advantage toward areas that remain difficult to automate, including strategy, culture, experiential marketing and real-world human connection. For marketers, the question becomes less about how to outperform the machine at optimization and more about where human judgment still creates differentiated value.

    [13:00] Shared Experiences Still Carry Outsized Value — Joe points to live events, festivals, hospitality and media tied to real-world experiences as areas with enduring value. His investment thesis reflects the belief that technology can help humans connect, but that physical spaces and shared cultural moments create something difficult to replicate digitally. For brands, that makes experiences and sponsorships more than awareness plays; they become part of the cultural infrastructure around the audience.

    [16:45] Brand Is Shared Cultural Currency — Joe rejects the performance marketing idea that every impression outside a narrow target audience is wasted. A brand needs to matter not only to the buyer, but also to the people around them – friends, family, colleagues, and wider culture. That shared narrative is part of what makes brand valuable, even when the effect cannot be captured neatly by last-click attribution.

    Industry observers note that [18:33] AI Changes the Incentive Problem, Not Just the Interface — Joe’s book Human Dot AI examines how the attention economy shaped the last 25 years through algorithms designed to decide what deserved people’s time. He believes the next phase is more consequential because conversational AI can build deeply personal relationships with users. His warning is that if those relationships are tied to performance or advertising incentives, marketers and consumers need to think carefully about who the AI is actually serving.

    Matt Britton is America’s leading expert on the millennial generation having consulted for over half of the Fortune 500 over the past two decades. He is the Founder and CEO of Suzy and the host of The Speed of Culture Podcast.

    Why Great Leaders ‘Clear the Runway’ ft. Alaska Airlines’ Eric Edge

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Transformation gets talked about like it’s a reinvention.
    • In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, Jenny Rooney welcomes Eric for an unpacking of what it takes to scale two heritage airline brands without flattening what made either one valuable.
    • He explains why Alaska and Hawaiian are operating under one airline group while remaining distinct consumer brands.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Transformation gets talked about like it’s a reinvention. But Eric Edge, VP of brand and marketing at Alaska Airlines, sees it differently.

    In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, Jenny Rooney welcomes Eric for an unpacking of what it takes to scale two heritage airline brands without flattening what made either one valuable.

    He explains why Alaska and Hawaiian are operating under one airline group while remaining distinct consumer brands.

    They also discuss what gave Alaska the right to expand globally, and why the fundamentals matter even more when the stakes get bigger.

    Eric Edge is VP of brand and marketing at Alaska Airlines, where he helps lead the brand strategy behind Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines as the two heritage brands expand their global footprint under one airline group.

    Sources indicate that his career began in the airline industry before moving into advertising and later technology, where he worked across Facebook, Instagram and Pinterest during major periods of digital transformation. Across those chapters, one theme has stayed consistent: strong fundamentals matter, but so does the curiosity to adapt when the rules change.

    Sources indicate that [04:13] The Leadership Lesson Eric Learned in the Chaos of Sept. 11 — Early in his career at United Airlines, Eric was part of the Flight 93 emergency response effort. In the middle of uncertainty, sorrow and incomplete information, he made a deliberate decision to focus on the mission in front of him and on helping those more deeply affected. That experience shaped a leadership mindset he still carries today and one that’s useful for marketers everywhere: control what you can control and do not let chaos immobilize you.

    In a recent development, [11:27] You Don’t Earn Global Ambition by Abandoning What Made You Good — Alaska’s move into routes like Rome, London, Seoul, Tokyo and Iceland was not built on reinvention for reinvention’s sake. Eric argues the firm earned the right to expand by first proving its operational performance, financial performance, culture of care and brand promise. The scale changed. The foundation did not.

    According to recent reports, [14:15] The “My Job Is to Clear the Runway” Leadership Principle — Eric sees leadership less as directing every move and more as removing whatever prevents people from doing their best work. He sets the vision, gives people ownership over outcomes and focuses on clearing blockers. The goal is not to become the center of every decision but rather make execution easier for the team.

    Industry observers note that [16:23] AI Isn’t the First Marketing Earthquake (And It Won’t Be the Last) — Eric wants marketers grounded in fundamentals but curious enough to accept that the tried and true may be disrupted. His own career included Facebook’s dramatic desktop-to-mobile pivot, a shift that felt existential at the time. AI is different, but his response is familiar: learn the new thing, experiment and use it to create more room for higher-stakes work.

    Jenny Rooney is Chief Brand and Community Officer, leading strategy for the overall ADWEEK brand as well as the ways in which we serve and support our audiences with high-value content, products, partnerships and experiences, notably through our community programs such as Marketing Vanguard.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adweek ↗ Open Full Page

    Q4 Isn’t the Offseason: Rethinking Active Audience Engagement and Brand Loyalty

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adweek

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • What if Q4 wasn’t the offseason for active consumers, but an opportunity for brands to connect with them in entirely newly introduced ways?
    • As temperatures drop and outdoor activities change, consumer behavior shifts rather than disappears.
    • For marketers, understanding these seasonal patterns is key to building meaningful engagement, driving product discoverability, and creating brand value that extends well beyond the holiday shopping calendar.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    What if Q4 wasn’t the offseason for active consumers, but an opportunity for brands to connect with them in entirely newly introduced ways?

    As temperatures drop and outdoor activities change, consumer behavior shifts rather than disappears.

    For marketers, understanding these seasonal patterns is key to building meaningful engagement, driving product discoverability, and creating brand value that extends well beyond the holiday shopping calendar.

    In this episode of Adspeak by ADWEEK, host Jen Starr, director of North America at Strava and head of Strava for Business, sits down with Daniel Rosenberg, senior brand director at Oakley who heads brand activation andpPartnerships for Costa Del Mar.

    They explore how brands can rethink their Q4 marketing strategy, engage performance-driven audiences year-round, and build stronger connections through community, partnerships, and consumer insights.

    The conversation examines how winter activity trends challenge the assumption that athletic engagement slows down in colder months. Strava data reveals significant increases in yoga uploads, weight training, and virtual rides, highlighting how athletes adapt their routines as outdoor activities move indoors.

    The guests discuss how brands can use these behavioral insights to inform seasonal consumer engagement, from fitness campaigns and snow sports marketing to athlete partnerships and marathon sponsorships.

    It has been revealed that they also explore why brands need to offer more than Black Friday discounts and Cyber Week promotions to remain relevant. By adding genuine value throughout the year, staying meaningfully present in consumers’ lives, and making products easier to discover, marketers can build lasting relationships rather than temporary conversions.

    According to recent reports, daniel Rosenberg is a senior brand and marketing leader with more than a decade of experience at the intersection of sport, culture, and consumer behavior. He serves as Senior Brand Director for Oakley and Head of Brand Activations & Partnerships for Costa Del Mar at EssilorLuxottica North America. Previously, Daniel spent over ten years agency-side, developing integrated marketing programs for brands including Nike and Meta. His work focuses on building brand relevance, driving commercial growth, and creating authentic consumer engagement.

    Jen Starr is an award-winning sales leader with more than 20 years of experience connecting brands with the communities that matter most. She at the moment serves as Director, North America, for Strava for Business, helping brands engage with Strava’s global community of 195 million athletes. Previously, she held leadership roles at BuzzFeed and Nextdoor, building and leading high-performing enterprise teams. A passionate culture builder and advocate for diversity and inclusion, Jen has spoken at SXSW, CES, the NYSE, and Cannes.

    [01:13] Q4 Is an Opportunity, Not an Off-Season — Consumer activity doesn’t disappear in winter; it simply changes shape. Strava data shows yoga uploads rising 35%, weight training 41%, and virtual rides 150% as athletes move indoors. Jen and Daniel explain why marketers should follow these shifts rather than pull back their Q4 marketing efforts. For brands like Oakley, staying relevant means showing up across running, skiing, and indoor training, wherever consumers choose to stay active.

    [04:04] Don’t Let Discounts Define Your Brand — Relying on Black Friday and Cyber Week promotions to attract first-time customers risks reducing a brand to little more than a discount. Daniel explains why lasting consumer relationships need to be built throughout the year, not just during peak shopping seasons. By staying connected to athletes through everyday training and competition, Oakley creates genuine brand value. The goal is to make holiday conversions an extension of existing loyalty, not simply a response to lower prices.

    [05:16] The Three Keys to Winning the Holiday Season — Successful holiday marketing requires more than attractive promotions. Daniel outlines three essentials: add value year-round, stay meaningfully present in consumers’ daily lives, and make products easy to discover. He explains how brands can integrate product storytelling into existing routines and interests without making every interaction feel transactional. For marketers, this provides a practical framework for balancing performance marketing and commercial objectives with authentic consumer engagement during Black Friday, Cyber Week, and beyond.

    [06:34] Why Community Beats Traditional Advertising — Consumers are more likely to engage with brands that enhance their experiences than those that simply compete for their attention. Daniel explains how community-driven marketing can create stronger connections than conventional advertising placements. Oakley’s first Q4 partnership with Strava brings this thinking to life through challenges and activations that reward participation and performance. The lesson for marketers is that successful platform partnerships should give audiences something meaningful rather than simply deliver another advertising impression.

    It has been revealed that [08:04] Think Ahead, But Deliver Value Today — Long-term brand building doesn’t have to come at the expense of immediate consumer relevance. Daniel shares Oakley’s guiding philosophy of designing for the future while delivering in the present. He explains how combining data with direct observation of athlete behavior helps inform marketing and creative decisions. The Travis Scott collaboration illustrates how brands can bring future-facing ideas into current cultural conversations, creating meaningful engagement while keeping today’s consumer needs firmly in focus.

    Sources indicate that [09:20] Follow Consumer Behavior, Not the Marketing Calendar — Legacy brands stay relevant by adapting to how consumers actually behave rather than relying on established seasonal marketing patterns. Daniel explains why understanding moments like Upcoming Year’s fitness resolutions creates opportunities to connect with audiences when their motivations naturally change. For Oakley, that means supporting athletes through winter training, skiing, and new fitness goals. The takeaway for marketers is simple: consumer-led strategies build stronger brand relevance than calendar-driven campaigns.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    According to recent reports, most Kit creators don't have a dedicated Creator Growth Manager, and when their emails start landing in spam, they need someone who can find the cause quickly and explain it in plain language. We're looking for a Deliverability and Compliance Specialist to own deliverability support for that long tail of creators, run Kit's abuse desk, and make the compliance calls that protect the sending reputation every creator on Kit shares.

    According to recent reports, you'll also build the playbooks, training, and AI-assisted workflows that help Support and contractors handle more deliverability questions on their own, and you'll partner with our infrastructure engineers as we run more of our sending in-house. A creator can't build a lasting business if their emails don't arrive, so this work connects directly to our mission.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role for someone who likes digging through headers and bounce logs to find the real cause of a problem, can explain DMARC alignment to a first-time creator without jargon, and is comfortable making a firm call when a situation is gray. You don't wait for someone to tell you what needs fixing. You proactively spot opportunities, identify patterns, and take the initiative to improve deliverability before problems arise.

    You'll report to Alyssa Dulin, Director of Creator Success, and collaborate closely with:.

    Our Deliverability team: a Deliverability Lead who supports our highest-value accounts and leads deliverability education, and a Deliverability Specialist who onboards and ramps up large senders moving to Kit.

    Our infrastructure engineers, who run Kit's sending infrastructure.

    Our compliance and anti-abuse engineers, who build the automated checks that keep spammers off Kit.

    Product Specialists and the Support team, who handle the front line and escalate deliverability problems to you.

    Customer Success Managers (we call them Creator Growth Managers at Kit), Sales and Migrations, and Product Managers.

    First Week: Get set up in Kit, our admin tools, and our support and ticketing systems, and meet our distributed team in Get To Know You chats (GTKYs). Meet the deliverability team and get an introduction on the current projects. Read our deliverability playbooks and SOPs, and get access to the monitoring tools you'll use every day: Google Postmaster Tools, Microsoft SNDS, blocklist monitoring, and our internal delivery dashboards.

    First Month: Shadow the Deliverability team and Product Specialists on deliverability tickets, account approvals, and abuse reports, then start answering queue tickets with review. Join the daily monitoring rotation (blocklist delisting, Postmaster and delivery monitoring) and the weekly Deliverability team meeting. Learn how account approvals, compliance flags, and our in-house sending platform work. By the end of the month, work deliverability tickets and abuse reports on your own and send your first delisting requests. Project: build a recurring report showing the trending deliverability ticket reasons so we understand what’s causing how to reduce friction for customers and how to solve it.

    First Six Months: Own the deliverability support queue for creators without a dedicated CGM: spam-folder placement, bounces, authentication and DMARC setup, and escalations from Product Specialists. Own compliance end to end, from fresh-account approvals and compliance flags to pausing or closing accounts that put our shared reputation at risk.Run Kit's abuse desk. You'll write and share a strategy that covers coverage, response-time targets, escalation paths, and quality checks, then put it in place so routine spam, phishing, and blocklist reports follow clear SOPs while you take the hardest cases yourself. Be the go-to contact for day-to-day mailbox provider issues with Microsoft, Gmail, Yahoo, Comcast, and regional providers, and write an incident runbook for blocklistings and provider throttling. Track the queue with a simple scorecard (volume, first response time, and escalation rate) and share what you learn with the team. Run training sessions for Support and ship your first process or AI improvements, like cleaner ticket categorization or better account data for our AI support agent, so more deliverability tickets get solved without escalation..

    According to recent reports, first Year: Deliverability support is faster and more consistent for every creator on Kit, including the ones who never talk to a CGM. Your playbooks, help center articles, and AI-assisted workflows are what Support, CGMs, and contractors reach for first, and fewer tickets need to come to you. You've led at least one cross-team fix with infrastructure for a recurring problem you spotted in the queue, such as an alert when a creator's domain authentication breaks or a check for sudden signup spikes. You're helping shape the internal tooling and alerting our in-house sending needs, and you take part in industry groups like M3AAWG.

    Deep working knowledge of email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, alignment, and BIMI basics), plus the ability to read raw message headers and SMTP bounce and deferral codes.

    Hands-on use of Google Postmaster Tools and Microsoft SNDS/JMRP, and comfort working with major blocklists (Spamhaus, Abusix, Barracuda, Spamcop, and others) and their delisting processes.

    Data fluency: you can pull bounce, complaint, and engagement data together, find the root cause, and explain it so others can act on it.

    Hands-on abuse handling: you can work an abuse report or escalation start to finish, from finding the account and assessing the evidence to acting, replying to the reporter, and documenting the decision.

    Process building: you can turn repeat work into SOPs, playbooks, and quality checks that a contractor or teammate can follow.

    Clear, calm written communication with creators, teammates, and postmasters.

    Using AI tools to research, summarize, and draft, and helping teammates do the same, with the judgment to keep a person on final compliance calls.

    Experience with MTA logs or delivery observability tools (KumoMTA, PowerMTA, Postfix, Kibana/Elasticsearch, or SQL and BI tools like Mode).

    Familiarity with feedback loops, spam traps, list bombing, and bot-signup patterns.

    Familiarity with CAN-SPAM, CASL, and GDPR as they apply to marketing email.

    Experience with Intercom, HubSpot, or a similar ticketing tool.

    Experience building or tuning AI support workflows or macros.

    4+ years in email deliverability, compliance, trust and safety, or technical support at an ESP, mailbox provider, or high-volume sender.

    Handling escalated customer tickets end to end, including with customers who are frustrated.

    Making account-level compliance or abuse decisions, such as approving, suspending, or closing accounts.

    Working an abuse desk or abuse mailbox directly: spam and phishing complaints, provider and blocklist reports, and escalations.

    Leading the fix for a recurring deliverability or compliance problem that needed help from more than one team.

    Supporting senders on shared IP pools at an ESP.

    Setting abuse or trust and safety strategy, or directing contractors or vendors on a support or abuse queue.

    Working directly with mailbox provider postmaster teams.

    Participating in M3AAWG or other industry groups.

    Creating educational content, like help docs, training, workshops, or podcasts.

    Working with creators, digital entrepreneurs, or small businesses.

    You pick up problems that fall between teams without waiting for permission, and you follow them through until they're closed.

    You test a hypothesis against the evidence before you act, and you frame problems clearly enough that others trust your analysis.

    You protect the reputation every creator shares while staying fair and kind to the creator in front of you, and you help them understand the reasoning behind a decision.

    You turn what you learn into docs, templates, and training that others use, and you adjust how you teach to fit the audience.

    You hold a high bar for your work, and you push back respectfully, with data, when something puts our reputation at risk, even when Sales or leadership would prefer a different answer.

    You share in-progress work and risks early so the team can solve problems together.

    Treating deliverability as a set of macros rather than an investigation that needs judgment.

    Discomfort saying no to a creator or a teammate when our shared reputation is at stake.

    Waiting for someone to assign you work when you can already see the problem.

    Needing a fixed playbook, since our sending stack and processes are changing as we bring more sending in-house.

    Keeping knowledge in your head instead of writing it down for the next person.

    Preferring to work without AI tools.

    Recent findings suggest that we're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time - so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    For this role, we're looking for someone based in North America, with working hours that give us solid US time zone coverage of the deliverability queue.

    According to recent reports, kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we're hiring at our level 3 ($118,000 USD). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    We cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance aims through Aetna.

    $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Company-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Industry observers note that winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.
